For product identification, we used an UHPLC (Thermo Scientific Dionex Ultimate 3000) coupled to a Thermo Scientific Q Exactive mass spectrometer - with the same chromatography method as described above. The MS parameters were set as follows: MS full-scan: range: 100–1500 m/z, resolution: 140 000, AGC target: 106, Maximum IT: 100 ms, positive electrospray ionization (tune data: capillary temperature: 275 °C, sheath gas: 15, aux gas: 10, sweep gas: 1, S-lens RF: 50.0), MS/MS acquisitions: Top5, resolution: 17 500, AGC target: 105, Maximum IT: 50 ms, isolation window: 1.0 m/z, NCE (stepped): 10, 20, 30, dynamic exclusion time: 2.0 s.

steps.title: Prepare derivatization reagents
steps.instruction: Make a 4 mM benzoin solution in ethanol, a 1.6 M aqueous KOH solution, and a 4.8 M aqueous HCl solution. Do not add β‑mercaptoethanol or sodium sulfite, as they are omitted in the final method.

steps.title: Derivatize sample
steps.instruction: For each 150 µL aqueous sample, cool to 0 °C in a 0.5 mL Protein LoBind tube, add 75 µL benzoin solution (4 mM), 75 µL water, and 150 µL KOH (1.6 M), invert three times, heat in a stirred boiling water bath (max 32 tubes) for 10 min, cool in an ice bath for 2 min, add 25 µL HCl (4.8 M), mix, transfer to a 1.5 mL Safe‑Lock tube, centrifuge at 10 000 g for 2 min, transfer the supernatant to a glass HPLC vial and store at –20 °C until LC‑MS analysis. If the guanidine concentration is >5 µM, dilute the supernatant with water to ≤5 µM before analysis.

steps.title: Set up HPLC‑MS/MS system
steps.instruction: Install an Agilent 1290 Infinity II UHPLC with an InfinityLab Poroshell 120 Bonus‑RP column (2.7 µm, 2.1 × 150 mm). Set column temperature to 40 °C, flow rate to 0.4 mL min⁻¹, and injection volume to 2 µL. Prepare mobile phase A (purified water + 0.1 % v/v formic acid) and mobile phase B (acetonitrile + 0.1 % v/v formic acid). Program the gradient: 0–1.5 min 5 % B, 1.5–4 min linear to 61 % B, 4–4.5 min linear to 95 % B, 4.5–7 min hold 95 % B, 7–8 min linear to 5 % B, 8–10 min hold 5 % B. Set MS source to positive ESI with gas temperature 250 °C, gas flow 10 L min⁻¹, nebulizer 45 psi, sheath gas temperature 280 °C, sheath gas flow 11 L min⁻¹, capillary voltage 3.5 kV, nozzle voltage 0.5 kV. Divert the LC flow to waste from 0–3 min and 5–10 min.

steps.title: Acquire MS data
steps.instruction: Monitor the parent ion at m/z 252.2 and its product ions at m/z 182.1 (quantifier) and m/z 104.1 (qualifier) with a quantifier/qualifier ratio of 1:0.68. Record the signal at the retention time of 3.75 min.

steps.title: Optional UHPLC‑Q Exactive analysis
steps.instruction: If using a Thermo Scientific Dionex Ultimate 3000 UHPLC coupled to a Q Exactive, apply the same chromatography method as above. Set MS full‑scan range 100–1500 m/z, resolution 140 000, AGC target 1 × 10⁶, maximum IT 100 ms, positive ESI (capillary temperature 275 °C, sheath gas 15, aux gas 10, sweep gas 1, S‑lens RF 50). For MS/MS use Top‑5, resolution 17 500, AGC target 1 × 10⁵, max IT 50 ms, isolation window 1.0 m/z, stepped NCE 10/20/30, dynamic exclusion 2.0 s.

steps.title: Prepare calibration standards
steps.instruction: Prepare guanidine standards ranging from 50 nM to 10 µM in water, derivatize each as described in step 2, and analyze by the LC‑MS method. Generate a weighted (1/x) quadratic calibration curve (R² > 0.999) and calculate LOD = x̄ + 3σ and LLOQ = x̄ + 10σ using three blank derivatizations; the resulting LOD is 13.7 nM and LLOQ is 47.9 nM.

steps.title: Quantify samples
steps.instruction: Inject derivatized samples (2 µL) under the conditions of step 3–4, use the calibration curve from step 6 to determine guanidine concentrations, and apply matrix‑matched calibration if samples are urine, wastewater, or growth medium. Dilute samples exceeding 5 µM after derivatization to keep the measured concentration ≤5 µM.

description: While our adapted method enables detecting guanidine in complex biological and environmental samples down to concentrations in the range of 10 nM, further reduction of this detection limit may be necessary to detect and quantify naturally occurring guanidine in environments such as soil or seawater, which may exhibit low steady-state concentrations. Beyond optimizing derivatization-based methods, an alternative approach could involve the direct analysis of guanidine using mass spectrometry, coupled with front-end separation by hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) and pre-reduction of high salt concentrations. Lastly, we note that further adaptations of the chromatography method (e.g., using a shorter column) can reduce the required analysis time and the amount of used solvent.
